issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Rajesh is a 64-year-old South Asian man who has worked the night shift in a warehouse for nearly two decades. He is married, with adult children who live in another state, and he has always prided himself on his reliability and physical stamina. That changed two years ago, when he was held captive for twelve hours in a shipping container by a group of men who had broken into the warehouse. They bound his hands and feet, gagged him, and left him in the dark. For hours, he lay on the cold metal floor, unable to move or call for help, listening to the sounds of rats scurrying nearby. He remembers the way the darkness felt absolute, and how his mind kept returning to a single thought: that no one would find him until it was too late. He was certain he could hear a snake slithering somewhere in the shadows, though he never saw one. When a security guard finally opened the container at dawn, Rajesh was trembling and covered in sweat. He told himself he was fine, that he had survived, and that he could put it behind him.

But he could not. Over the following weeks, Rajesh found that the time of day had become a trigger he could not escape. Every evening, as the clock approached the hour when he had been taken, his body would tense and his heart would pound. The onset of darkness, especially waking up in the middle of the night, brought the same visceral dread. He began to avoid going to sleep, lying in bed with the lights on, his eyes fixed on the ceiling, until exhaustion finally pulled him under. When his wife asked why he was so restless, he would say he was just having trouble sleeping, but privately he had started asking her, again and again, whether he was safe, whether the doors were locked, whether she thought he was okay. She would reassure him, but the relief never lasted. He also found himself running his hands over his arms and legs, checking for cuts or bruises, as though his body might be hiding an injury he had not noticed. These maladaptive strategies—the avoidance of sleep, the constant reassurance-seeking, the body monitoring—became his nightly routine, and they only deepened his sense of helplessness. Lying awake, he would tell himself that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, that his life was not worth living anymore, and that if he allowed himself to think about the event, he would not be able to handle it.

The triggers also kept his threat system on high alert. At night, Rajesh found it harder to feel safe than during the day; he was superalert, watchful, and on guard. He frequently looked behind him to check if someone was following him, even in his own home. When he heard a creak in the hallway, his mind would leap to the image of the container door sliding shut. The hypervigilance was exhausting, but he could not turn it off. His negative appraisals—the belief that he was helpless, that his life had lost its value, that his own thoughts were dangerous—fed directly into this state of threat. He was certain that he was not safe, that he could not protect himself, and that the world was full of hidden dangers he would not see coming. This conviction made his nights unbearable.

Over the months, the cycle tightened. His maladaptive strategies—the sleepless nights, the endless checking, the pleas for reassurance—left him depleted and ashamed. He began to believe that he was weak, that he had failed to handle the event, and that he would never recover. These negative appraisals, in turn, made the triggers more potent. The same time of day now carried not just fear but a crushing sense of hopelessness. The dark no longer just frightened him; it confirmed that his life was not worth living. And because he avoided sleep, he was awake to experience the triggers, night after night, in a relentless loop.

Rajesh finally sought help after his wife found him in the living room at three in the morning, sitting in the dark with his eyes wide open, his hands trembling. He told her he was checking his body for a wound he was sure was there. What frightened him most was not the memory of the container, but the thought that he would never feel safe again, and that the darkness would always be waiting.
